5.6 Pseudocode summary of the finite element procedure
The program follows three main stages: pre-processing, processing, and post-processing. The processing stage is further divided into assembly, application of the boundary conditions, and solution.
1. Pre-processing: Input Data
   - Define the number of nodes and displacement degrees of freedom per node
   - Define the element connectivity
   - Define the stiffness of each spring element
   - Define the constrained degrees of freedom
   - Define the applied nodal forces
   - Compute the total number of degrees of freedom and elements
   - Initialize the global stiffness matrix K
   - Initialize the global force vector f

2. Processing

   2.1 Assembly: Build Global K
       - For each element:
         - Read the element stiffness k_e
         - Construct the element stiffness matrix K_e
         - Build the local-to-global degree-of-freedom map
         - Add the entries of K_e to the corresponding entries of K
       - Display the assembled global stiffness matrix K

   2.2 Boundary Conditions
       - Copy the assembled matrix K as K_original
       - Add the applied nodal forces to f
       - For each constrained degree of freedom:
         - Set the corresponding row and column of K to zero
         - Set the corresponding diagonal entry of K to one
         - Set the corresponding entry of f to zero

   2.3 Solver
       - Solve the modified linear system K u = f
       - Display the computed and analytical displacement vectors for comparison

3. Post-processing: Strain Energy
   - Compute the total internal strain energy from
     1/2 u^T K_original u
   - Compute the analytical strain energy
   - Compare the numerical and analytical energy values

5.7 Walkthrough of the Julia script
The Julia language features used below were introduced in Chapter 2. In this walkthrough we identify the finite element meaning of each data structure and computational step.

5.7.1 Model dimensions and input data
The model dimensions are
num_nodes = 3
dofs_per_node = 1
total_dofs = num_nodes * dofs_per_node
As there is one displacement degree of freedom per node, total_dofs is equal to 3.
The element connectivity is stored as a matrix:
element_connectivity = [
    2 3;
    3 1
]
Each row represents one element. The first and second columns contain the global nodes associated with local nodes 1 and 2:








element number
global node corresponding to local node 1
global node corresponding to local node 2




1
2
3


2
3
1



The spring stiffnesses are stored in the same element order:
element_stiffness = [1.0, 2.0]
meaning that element_stiffness[1] belongs to element 1 and element_stiffness[2] belongs to element 2.






ImportantConsistent units



The script stores physical quantities as ordinary numerical values; it does not attach or check units. The input data must therefore use a consistent unit system. In this example, forces are in newtons, lengths in millimeters, spring stiffnesses in newtons per millimeter, and strain energy in newton millimeters.


The number of elements is obtained from the number of rows in the connectivity matrix:
num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)
The applied force and homogeneous displacement constraint are represented by
applied_force = 10.0
applied_forces = [(1, applied_force)]
constrained_dofs = [2]
Each entry of applied_forces associates a global degree-of-freedom index with a force value. Here, the force acts at global degree of freedom 1.
The vector constrained_dofs contains the index of the constrained degree of freedom. Because the prescribed displacement is zero in this first snapshot, there is no need for a data structure analogous to applied_forces; the code therefore stores only the constrained degree-of-freedom index.






ImportantNumerical order is not geometric order



The physical nodes are arranged from left to right as 2 -> 3 -> 1, whereas the global arrays follow numerical order. Consequently,
u[1] = displacement of the rightmost node
u[2] = displacement of the fixed left node
u[3] = displacement of the internal node








NoteArray indices and model identifiers



In this script, global degree-of-freedom numbers are used directly as Julia array indices. The internal degree-of-freedom numbering must therefore form the consecutive sequence
1, 2, ..., total_dofs
External mesh or data-file labels do not need to follow this rule. Arbitrary labels such as 3, 4, 5, 99 can be retained, provided that they are mapped to consecutive internal indices such as 1, 2, 3, 4 before the algebraic arrays are constructed.




5.7.2 Global arrays
The global stiffness matrix and force vector are initialized as zero-filled arrays:
K = zeros(total_dofs, total_dofs)
f = zeros(total_dofs)
For this problem, K is a 3 x 3 matrix and f is a vector with three entries. They begin at zero because element stiffness contributions and applied nodal forces will be accumulated into them.


5.7.3 Element loop
The assembly stage visits each spring element in turn. The computational part of the element loop is
for e in 1:num_elements
    k_e = element_stiffness[e]
    K_e = [
        +k_e -k_e;
        -k_e +k_e
    ]

    dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

    for i in 1:2
        I = dof_map[i]
        for j in 1:2
            J = dof_map[j]
            K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
        end
    end
end
For each element, the script retrieves its stiffness, constructs its element stiffness matrix, builds the local-to-global degree-of-freedom map, and adds the element contribution to the global stiffness matrix. One iteration of this loop therefore performs the element-level operations required by the direct stiffness procedure.


5.7.4 Constructing the element matrix
For the current element, the stiffness value is retrieved with
k_e = element_stiffness[e]
and the mathematical element matrix
\[
  \mathbf{K}^{(e)}=k_e
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & -1\\
  -1 & 1
  \end{bmatrix}
\]
is represented by
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
K_e contains the stiffness matrix of the current element and must not be confused with the assembled global matrix K.


5.7.5 Building the local-to-global map
For element e, the global degrees of freedom are read from the connectivity matrix:
dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]
The resulting maps are
element 1: dof_map = [2, 3]
element 2: dof_map = [3, 1]
Because the model has one degree of freedom per node, the connected node numbers are also the global degree-of-freedom numbers. This equivalence will no longer hold automatically when several degrees of freedom are attached to each node.
The two entries of dof_map correspond, in order, to local degrees of freedom 1 and 2. The map therefore identifies the global rows and columns into which the entries of K_e are assembled.


5.7.6 Assembling the global stiffness matrix
The element matrix must be transferred from its local ordering to the global matrix ordering. Suppose that the local degrees of freedom \(\{1,2\}\) correspond to the global degrees of freedom \(\{2,3\}\):
local degree of freedom:   1   2
global degree of freedom:  2   3
This correspondence defines a local-to-global map
\[
  g(1)=2,
  \qquad
  g(2)=3.
\]
An entry of the element matrix is identified by a local row index and a local column index. For a two-degree-of-freedom element, all element entries are therefore represented by the Cartesian product
\[
  \{1,2\}\times\{1,2\}
  =
  \{(1,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,1),\ (2,2)\}.
\]
The local-to-global map is applied separately to the row and column indices:
\[
  (i,j)
  \longmapsto
  \bigl(g(i),g(j)\bigr).
\]
For element 1,
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  (1,1)&\longmapsto(2,2),\\
  (1,2)&\longmapsto(2,3),\\
  (2,1)&\longmapsto(3,2),\\
  (2,2)&\longmapsto(3,3).
  \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  K_{22} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{11},\\
  K_{23} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{12},\\
  K_{32} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{21},\\
  K_{33} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{22}.
  \end{aligned}
\]
The nested loops implement exactly this operation:
for i in 1:2
    I = dof_map[i]
    for j in 1:2
        J = dof_map[j]
        K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
    end
end
Lowercase i and j identify local row and column positions, whereas uppercase I and J identify the corresponding global positions. In mathematical form, the operation performed for every local pair is
\[
  K_{g(i),g(j)}\mathrel{+}=K^{(e)}_{ij}.
\]
The contribution is added rather than overwritten because different elements may contribute to the same global matrix entry. In this model, both elements contribute to K[3, 3].






TipExercise – Modify one element stiffness



Change the stiffness of element 2 from
element_stiffness = [1.0, 2.0]
to
element_stiffness = [1.0, 3.0]
Before running the script, predict which entries of the assembled global stiffness matrix K will change and which will remain unchanged.
Then run the script and compare the new matrix with the original one. Use the connectivity of element 2 and its local-to-global degree-of-freedom map to explain the result.
For this exercise, focus only on the assembled matrix K; the hard-coded analytical displacement later in the script corresponds to the original stiffness values.




5.7.7 Preserving the assembled matrix
Before the displacement condition modifies the global matrix, the script preserves the assembled physical stiffness matrix:
K_original = copy(K)
This distinction is important mechanically. K_original represents the assembled stiffness matrix before the displacement constraint is imposed, whereas K will subsequently be modified into the algebraic system matrix used by the solver. The original matrix is required for the strain-energy computation and can also be used to recover reactions.
The Julia semantics of copy were introduced in Chapter 2; here its purpose is to keep the original physical operator available after K is modified.


5.7.8 Assembling the applied force
The applied nodal-force data are transferred into the global vector with
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
For the current data, the resulting vector is
\[
  \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  10\\0\\0
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{N}.
\]
The support reaction is not entered as an applied load because it is unknown. It can be recovered after the displacement solution from the original equilibrium equations.


5.7.9 Imposing the homogeneous displacement constraint
The zero displacement at degree of freedom 2 is imposed with
for dof in constrained_dofs
    for i in 1:total_dofs
        K[i, dof] = 0.0
        K[dof, i] = 0.0
    end

    K[dof, dof] = 1.0
    f[dof] = 0.0
end
For each constrained degree of freedom, the code zeros the corresponding row and column, places one on the diagonal, and sets the corresponding right-hand side entry to zero. For the present problem, the modified system is
\[
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & 0\\
  -2 & 0 & 3
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\u_2\\u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  10\\0\\0
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its second equation is exactly \(u_2=0\).
In Chapter 4, the modified arrays were denoted by \(\widetilde{\mathbf{K}}\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}\). The script does not introduce new variable names for them: K and f are modified in place. After this operation, K represents the modified algebraic system matrix rather than the original physical stiffness matrix. The original assembled matrix remains available as K_original.






NoteScope of this implementation



This row-and-column modification is sufficient for a homogeneous prescribed displacement. A nonzero prescribed value also requires a consistent correction of the right-hand side and is introduced in a later snapshot.




5.7.10 Solving the linear system
The modified system is solved with
u = K \ f
which computes the solution of
\[
  \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}.
\]
The backslash operator was introduced in Chapter 2. Its finite element role here is simply to solve the constrained global equilibrium system for the unknown nodal displacements.


5.7.11 Comparing displacement results
The reference displacement vector is stored in global order:
u_analytical = [15.0, 0.0, 10.0]
and is displayed alongside the numerical solution for comparison.


5.7.12 Computing the internal strain energy
The numerical internal strain energy is computed with the original assembled matrix:
strain_energy_global = 0.5 * transpose(u) * K_original * u
This is the Julia representation of
\[
  U=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}
  \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{original}}\mathbf{u}.
\]
The independent reference value is computed from the two spring stiffnesses:
k_1 = element_stiffness[1]
k_2 = element_stiffness[2]
strain_energy_analytical = 0.5 * applied_force^2 * (1 / k_1 + 1 / k_2)
The derivation of this expression is given in Chapter 4. The important point here is that the numerical energy uses the original assembled stiffness matrix, not the matrix after the displacement constraint has been inserted.

5.8 Verification
A program result should not be accepted merely because the script runs. The present example provides several checks against quantities already derived independently.

5.8.1 Assembled stiffness matrix
Before boundary conditions, the expected global matrix is
\[
  \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{expected}}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & -1\\
  -2 & -1 & 3
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{N/mm}.
\]
The matrix should be symmetric, and each row should sum to zero before displacement constraints are imposed, reflecting the rigid-translation mode of the unconstrained assembly.


5.8.2 Displacements
The numerical solution should be
\[
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  15\\0\\10
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
Remember that the entries are in global numerical order. The rightmost node is the first entry, the fixed left node is the second, and the internal node is the third.


5.8.3 Element elongations and spring forces
Using the element connectivity,
\[
  \delta_1=u_3-u_2=10\ \mathrm{mm},
  \qquad
  \delta_2=u_1-u_3=5\ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
  F_s^{(1)}=k_1\delta_1=10\ \mathrm{N},
  \qquad
  F_s^{(2)}=k_2\delta_2=10\ \mathrm{N}.
\]
The equal internal spring forces confirm equilibrium at the internal node.


5.8.4 Internal strain energy
Both the global quadratic form and the independent spring expression should give
\[
  U=75\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
\]
The script reports the absolute difference between the numerical and analytical energy values. For this small problem, the difference should be zero or a very small value arising from floating-point rounding. Approximate comparisons and numerical tolerances are discussed in Part II of Chapter 2.
Recovery of the support reaction provides one further equilibrium check and is left as Exercise 3.

6.1 Starting point
In Chapter 5, the direct stiffness procedure was translated into the first MiniFEM Julia script. The resulting program is intentionally explicit: the input data, element operations, assembly, boundary conditions, solution, and post-processing all appear directly in the top-level script. This makes the numerical procedure easy to follow line by line. However, several parts of the program now represent well-defined operations that can be given names of their own. For example, the element stiffness matrix is constructed directly inside the element loop:
Similarly, global assembly, force assembly, application of the displacement constraint, and strain-energy computation are all written directly where they are used.
We will use the final code from the previous snapshot as our starting point and refactor its implementation without changing the finite element calculation.

6.2 Goal of this snapshot
The goal of this snapshot is to refactor the existing two-spring program using Julia functions.
The mechanical problem, finite element formulation, input data, boundary conditions, and numerical results will remain unchanged. The implementation will be reorganized into functions, and some diagnostic output will be simplified.
By the end of the snapshot, the following finite element operations will have their own functions:
spring_stiffness
assemble_stiffness!
assemble_forces!
apply_homogeneous_constraints!
strain_energy
The top-level part of the script will then describe the overall finite element workflow by calling the higher-level functions, while assemble_stiffness! will use spring_stiffness internally.
The refactored program must reproduce exactly the same numerical results as the starting snapshot. We will verify this after completing the refactoring.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.3 From operations to functions
The syntax for defining and calling Julia functions was introduced in Section 2.3.6. We now apply those ideas to the existing two-spring implementation.
Our approach will be incremental. For each finite element operation, we will first identify the corresponding block of code in the starting snapshot and move that code into a function with as little modification as possible. We will then replace the original block with a call to the new function. We will consider further improvements to the function only after this direct extraction.
Two types of functions will appear in this snapshot:

functions that compute and return a result;
functions that modify an existing object supplied as an argument.

The distinction will become clear as we refactor the code.
As each function is introduced below, place its definition before the top-level pre-processing section. The finite element functions will therefore remain grouped together, followed by the top-level analysis that calls them.
Variables introduced inside the extracted functions are local to those functions, following the function-scope rules introduced in Section 2.3.6. This allows each operation to manage its own temporary quantities without exposing them to the top-level analysis.

section: 6.4 First step: extract the element stiffness operation
text:
6.4 First step: extract the element stiffness operation
A useful way to introduce functions into an existing program is to begin with a small, self-contained operation.
In the previous snapshot, the element stiffness matrix is constructed inside the element loop:
k_e = element_stiffness[e]
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
The matrix construction depends only on k_e, so it can be moved directly into a function, as shown below.
Before
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
After
function spring_stiffness(k_e)
    K_e = [
        +k_e -k_e;
        -k_e +k_e
    ]
    return K_e
end
Place this function near the beginning of the file, immediately below the descriptive comment in the file header.
The original matrix construction inside the element loop is then replaced by
K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)
Nothing has changed mathematically. The same value of k_e produces the same matrix K_e: the operation has simply been given a name.
This is the first type of function introduced above: spring_stiffness receives the data required for the calculation and returns a new result. It does not modify k_e.
This first transformation illustrates an important refactoring principle used throughout this snapshot:

first move an existing operation into a function without changing how the operation itself is performed.

Once the function works, its interface can be considered separately.
Before attempting the next refactoring step, run the program and confirm that it produces the same numerical results as before.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.5 Extracting global stiffness assembly
The next operation is larger. After extracting the element stiffness operation, global stiffness assembly is still performed by the complete element loop:
for e in 1:num_elements
    # Element stiffness matrix: K_e = k_e * [1 -1; -1 1]
    k_e = element_stiffness[e]
    K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)

    println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
    println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
    display(K_e)

    # Map local DOFs to global DOFs for an element:
    # the local to global DOF mapping is built from element nodes
    # through the element connectivity matrix (for elements with one DOF
    # per node, the global DOF is the same as the node number).
    dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

    # Assemble the local stiffness matrix into the global stiffness matrix.
    for i in 1:2
        I = dof_map[i]
        for j in 1:2
            J = dof_map[j]
            K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
        end
    end
end
At this stage, keep the loop unchanged and place it inside a function:
function assemble_stiffness!(
    K,
    element_connectivity,
    element_stiffness,
    num_elements,
)
    for e in 1:num_elements
        # Element stiffness matrix: K_e = k_e * [1 -1; -1 1]
        k_e = element_stiffness[e]
        K_e = spring_stiffness(k_e)

        println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
        println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
        display(K_e)

        # Map local DOFs to global DOFs for an element:
        # the local to global DOF mapping is built from element nodes
        # through the element connectivity matrix (for elements with one DOF
        # per node, the global DOF is the same as the node number).
        dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

        # Assemble the local stiffness matrix into the global stiffness matrix.
        for i in 1:2
            I = dof_map[i]
            for j in 1:2
                J = dof_map[j]
                K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
            end
        end
    end
end
The original element loop can now be replaced by
assemble_stiffness!(
    K,
    element_connectivity,
    element_stiffness,
    num_elements,
)
Again, the assembly algorithm itself has not changed. The nested loops, the local-to-global map, and the additive update of K are exactly the operations used in the previous snapshot.
Unlike spring_stiffness, this function does not construct and return a new global matrix. It modifies the existing matrix K through the accumulated assignment
K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
For this reason, the function is named assemble_stiffness!. As introduced in Section 2.3.6, the trailing ! is a Julia naming convention used to signal that a function modifies one or more of its arguments; the ! does not itself cause the modification.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.6 Choosing function arguments
The first version of assemble_stiffness! reproduces the existing assembly operation with as little modification as possible. We can now move from direct extraction to a small refinement of its interface by inspecting its arguments.
The function currently receives
num_elements
but the number of elements can already be determined from
element_connectivity
using
size(element_connectivity, 1)
Passing both pieces of information creates unnecessary duplication. To remove this redundancy, move the calculation
num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)
inside the function:
function assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)
    num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)

    # element loop
end
The call then becomes
assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)
and the top-level definition of num_elements is no longer required.
This gives a useful guideline for designing function interfaces:

pass the information required to perform an operation, but avoid passing a quantity that can be obtained unambiguously from information already available to the function.

This is a guideline rather than an absolute rule. Later implementations may make different choices for reasons of efficiency or software design.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
section: 6.7 Keeping numerical operations separate from printed output
text:
6.7 Keeping numerical operations separate from printed output
The first extracted assembly function still contains the diagnostic output from the starting script:
println("\n-- Element ", e, ", k_e = ", k_e)
println("   Element stiffness matrix K_e:")
display(K_e)
These statements were useful in the first snapshot because the intermediate element matrices were deliberately exposed while introducing assembly. The purpose of assemble_stiffness!, however, is to perform the numerical assembly itself. Displaying intermediate results is a separate task: it does not contribute to the assembly operation and need not be part of the function.
You can therefore remove these three statements from assemble_stiffness! and let the top-level script report the beginning and result of the assembly operation:
println("\n- Assembling local stiffness matrices into global K")
assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)

println("\n- Global stiffness matrix K:")
display(K)
The numerical calculation has not changed; only the diagnostic output produced inside the assembly loop has been removed. This keeps the numerical operation separate from the decision about what information should be displayed to the user.
This is an example of separation of concerns: the numerical function is responsible for performing the assembly, while decisions about diagnostic output are kept outside the function.

text:
6.8 Extracting force assembly
The applied nodal forces are still assembled directly in the top-level script:
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
This is already a small, self-contained operation.
Move it directly into
function assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
    for (dof, value) in applied_forces
        f[dof] += value
    end
end
and replace the original loop with
assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
The function modifies f, so its name follows the ! convention.
Notice also that the function does not need to know anything about springs. It only receives a global force vector and a collection of degree-of-freedom/value pairs.
This is the first indication that some of the operations being extracted from the two-spring example are more general than the particular mechanical problem that introduced them.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.9 Extracting the displacement constraint
The homogeneous prescribed displacement is still imposed directly in the top-level script:
for dof in constrained_dofs
    for i in 1:total_dofs
        K[i, dof] = 0.0
        K[dof, i] = 0.0
    end

    K[dof, dof] = 1.0
    f[dof] = 0.0
end
As before, begin with a direct extraction:
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)
    for dof in constrained_dofs
        for i in 1:total_dofs
            K[i, dof] = 0.0
            K[dof, i] = 0.0
        end

        K[dof, dof] = 1.0
        f[dof] = 0.0
    end
end
The original loop can then be replaced by
apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)
The function modifies both K and f, which again motivates the trailing !.

6.9.1 Refining the arguments
As with num_elements in the assembly function, one of the arguments can be obtained from information already available to the function.
The number of global degrees of freedom is equal to the number of rows of K, so it can be determined directly from the matrix:
total_dofs = size(K, 1)
There is therefore no need to pass total_dofs as a separate argument. Move this calculation inside the function.
The function definition therefore changes from
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
    total_dofs,
)

    # constraint loop
end
to
function apply_homogeneous_constraints!(
    K,
    f,
    constrained_dofs,
)
    total_dofs = size(K, 1)

    # constraint loop
end
and the corresponding call becomes
apply_homogeneous_constraints!(K, f, constrained_dofs)
Unlike num_elements, the top-level variable total_dofs is still required elsewhere in the script to initialize the global arrays:
K = zeros(total_dofs, total_dofs)
f = zeros(total_dofs)
It therefore remains part of the pre-processing stage. The total_dofs defined inside apply_homogeneous_constraints! is local to that function and is separate from the top-level variable with the same name.

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.10 Extracting the strain-energy computation
The global strain energy is still computed directly in the top-level script:
strain_energy_global = 0.5 * transpose(u) * K_original * u
Extract this operation into a function that receives a stiffness matrix and a displacement vector and returns the corresponding strain energy:
function strain_energy(K, u)
    return 0.5 * transpose(u) * K * u
end
and replace the original expression with
strain_energy_global = strain_energy(K_original, u)
The analytical reference calculation remains in the top-level script because it is specific to the two-spring benchmark:
k_1 = element_stiffness[1]
k_2 = element_stiffness[2]
strain_energy_analytical =
    0.5 * applied_force^2 * (1 / k_1 + 1 / k_2)
The same applies to the analytical displacement vector:
u_analytical = [15.0, 0.0, 10.0]
These quantities are used to verify the finite element solution rather than to define reusable finite element operations.
Before finishing the refactoring, clean up the comments so that they describe the new program structure rather than the original top-level implementation. Update headings and descriptive comments where necessary, add concise comments for the new function block, and remove comments that have become redundant. These changes affect the documentation only, not the executable code.

6.11 Structure of the refactored program
The mathematical sequence of the program has not changed. The main difference is that several finite element operations now have explicit names:
Pre-processing

    initialize K and f

Processing
    assemble_stiffness!(...)
    preserve K_original
    assemble_forces!(...)
    apply_homogeneous_constraints!(...)

Verification

title: 6  Organizing finite element operations with functions
text:
6.12 What changed?
The finite element procedure itself has not changed. What has changed is where the details of each operation are expressed.
In the starting snapshot, the top-level script describes directly how an operation is performed. For example:
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
After refactoring, the top-level script instead states what operation should be performed:
assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
The implementation has not disappeared; it has moved into a named function.
The same transition has been made for stiffness assembly, application of the homogeneous constraints, and strain-energy computation. The top-level script therefore exposes the finite element procedure more clearly, while the detailed implementation remains available in the function definitions.

6.13 Verification after refactoring
Refactoring should not alter the numerical problem being solved.
Run the modified program and verify that the assembled stiffness matrix is still
\[
  \mathbf{K}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & -1\\
  -2 & -1 & 3

\]

  15\\
  0\\
  10
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm},
\]
and the numerical strain energy should remain

\]

Calling a complete analysis makes it possible to request results for new physical input values without repeating the finite element workflow at every call site. The analysis remains visible in the code, but it is now grouped together as one operation with a defined interface.

7.3 What varies and what remains fixed
For this two-spring benchmark, three physical quantities vary:
k_1
k_2
applied_force
The topology remains fixed: the physical nodes are numbered 2, 3, and 1 from left to right; the spring connectivity is (2, 3) and (3, 1); and node 2 has a homogeneous prescribed displacement. These choices belong to this particular benchmark, so they remain inside the callable analysis.
The result is deliberately not a generic MiniFEM solver. It is a reusable analysis for one specific, already-understood two-spring problem.

title: 7  Making the two-spring analysis callable
text:
7.4 Introducing solve_two_springs
The callable analysis receives the three varying physical quantities:
function solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force)
Inside the function, the existing finite element workflow is preserved: problem definition, assembly, application of boundary conditions, solution, and post-processing remain in the same order as before.
The corresponding function is:
function solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force)
    # Fixed topology: physical nodes are labeled [2, 3, 1] from left to right.
    num_nodes = 3
    dofs_per_node = 1

    element_connectivity = [
        2 3;
        3 1
    ]

    constrained_dofs = [2]
    element_stiffness = [k_1, k_2]
    applied_forces = [(1, applied_force)]

    total_dofs = num_nodes * dofs_per_node
    K = zeros(total_dofs, total_dofs)
    f = zeros(total_dofs)

    assemble_stiffness!(K, element_connectivity, element_stiffness)

    # Preserve the physical stiffness matrix before Dirichlet modification.
    K_original = copy(K)

    assemble_forces!(f, applied_forces)
    apply_homogeneous_constraints!(K, f, constrained_dofs)

    u = K \ f
    strain_energy_global = strain_energy(K_original, u)

    return u, strain_energy_global
end
The copy of K is needed because applying the homogeneous constraint modifies the system matrix, while the strain energy must be computed using the original assembled stiffness matrix.

text:
7.5 Returning the displacement vector and strain energy
The analysis returns two quantities:
return u, strain_energy_global
Here u is the complete global displacement vector, and strain_energy_global is the total internal strain energy. The Julia variable strain_energy_global corresponds to the mathematical total strain energy denoted by \(U\). The returned tuple can be destructured using the syntax introduced in Chapter 2:
u, strain_energy_global = solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force)
The complete vector u is returned rather than only one selected displacement. The vector is the finite element solution of the global system, and later analyses may require different displacement components. A selected physical response can always be extracted from the complete result when needed.

text:
7.9 What the new organization enables
The refactoring changes only the organization of the program. The mechanical model and numerical results remain unchanged. The callable analysis can now be invoked repeatedly with different values of k_1, k_2, and applied_force. The exercise below uses this ability for a small parameter study. In the next implementation snapshot, the returned quantities u and strain_energy_global will also provide meaningful targets for automated regression tests.






TipExercise — A stiffness-allocation study



Use solve_two_springs to study how the response changes when the total spring stiffness remains fixed:
\[
  k_1+k_2=k_{\mathrm{total}},
\]
with
\[
  k_1=\alpha k_{\mathrm{total}},
  \qquad
  k_2=(1-\alpha)k_{\mathrm{total}},
  \qquad
  0<\alpha<1.
\]
Use the following study inputs:
k_total = 3.0
applied_force = 10.0
Study values of \(\alpha\) from 0.1 to 0.9 in increments of 0.1. Create a variable named alpha_values yourself using one of the range constructions introduced in Chapter 2.
Work through the following steps.

Confirm that alpha_values contains values strictly between 0 and 1.
Use length(alpha_values) to determine the number of analyses.
Preallocate a numerical matrix named results with one row per value of alpha and three columns using zeros. Use the columns in this order:
alpha | u_loaded | U
Use an indexed for loop of the form for i in 1:length(alpha_values) to call solve_two_springs once for each value of alpha. Keep the parameter study outside solve_two_springs.
Within each iteration, obtain alpha from alpha_values[i], compute k_1 and k_2, call solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force), and assign the two returned values to u and strain_energy_global.
The physical displacement of interest is the displacement at the loaded end. Call it u_loaded. Because this benchmark uses the deliberately nonsequential physical node ordering [2, 3, 1], the loaded node is global DOF 1. Extract it from the returned vector as u_loaded = u[1].
Store the Julia variables alpha, u_loaded, and the returned strain_energy_global in row i of results. When the loop is complete, display that matrix.
Verify the computed entries against the analytical solution. For a force \(F\), the two springs in series give
\[
  u_{\mathrm{loaded}}
  = F\left(\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}\right),
  \qquad
  U
  = \frac{F^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}\right).
\]
In these equations, \(U\) is the mathematical strain-energy symbol. In the Julia code, the corresponding returned value is strain_energy_global; use applied_force for the quantity denoted by \(F\).
Interpret the results. At which value of \(\alpha\) are the loaded displacement and strain energy smallest? Is the response symmetric about \(\alpha=0.5\)? What happens as \(\alpha\) approaches 0 or 1, and why must those endpoint values be excluded from the numerical study?

No plot is required for this exercise.

8  From analytical verification to regression testing

title: 8  From analytical verification to regression testing
text:
8.2 Verification, validation, and regression testing
Verification and validation answer different questions. Verification asks whether the numerical implementation correctly solves the mathematical model. Validation asks whether that mathematical model represents the physical system sufficiently well for its intended use.
The analytical two-spring solution used here provides a verification reference: it checks the finite element result against an independently derived solution of the same idealized spring model. Agreement establishes confidence in the formulation and implementation for this problem, but it does not validate the spring model against physical behavior.
Regression testing asks a different question: does previously verified behavior still agree with the established reference after later changes? A passing regression test does not prove that every FEM formulation is generally correct. A failing test means that protected behavior no longer matches its reference; it does not by itself identify the cause or decide which version is correct.

8.3 Separating the FEM implementation from the benchmark
In S03, the reusable finite element functions, solve_two_springs, and the executable canonical benchmark all lived in examples/two_springs.jl. This was appropriate while the file was used only as an executable example.
Regression testing creates a new requirement. The tests need to call solve_two_springs without also executing the benchmark presentation and analytical verification contained in two_springs.jl.
S04 therefore separates the reusable finite element implementation from the executable benchmark:
two_springs_fem.jl
    reusable finite element definitions

two_springs.jl
    executable benchmark, presentation, and analytical verification

test/runtests.jl
    automated regression checks
Both the executable benchmark and the tests include two_springs_fem.jl. The same finite element implementation can therefore be used in both contexts without duplicating the code or executing benchmark output during the tests.

text:
8.4 Introducing Test
The test file begins with:
using Test
A @testset groups related checks, and @test checks one expected condition. The two-spring results use floating-point arithmetic, so S04 uses isapprox with explicit absolute and relative tolerances:
atol = 1.0e-12
rtol = 1.0e-12
The roles of absolute and relative tolerance were introduced in Chapter 2. Here they make the intended numerical comparison explicit rather than relying on a default tolerance.
The function isapprox can also compare numerical arrays, so the complete displacement vector can be checked in one assertion.

title: 8  From analytical verification to regression testing
text:
8.5 The regression tests
The complete test file is:
using Test

include("../examples/two_springs_fem.jl")

@testset "Two-spring regression tests" begin
    atol = 1.0e-12
    rtol = 1.0e-12

    # Canonical two-spring benchmark
    k_1 = 1.0
    k_2 = 2.0
    applied_force = 10.0
    u_expected = [15.0, 0.0, 10.0]
    strain_energy_expected = 75.0

    u, strain_energy_global = solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force)

    @test isapprox(u, u_expected; atol=atol, rtol=rtol)
    @test isapprox(
        strain_energy_global,
        strain_energy_expected;
        atol=atol,
        rtol=rtol,
    )

    # Noncanonical two-spring benchmark
    k_1 = 2.0
    k_2 = 3.0
    applied_force = 12.0
    u_expected = [10.0, 0.0, 6.0]
    strain_energy_expected = 60.0

    u, strain_energy_global = solve_two_springs(k_1, k_2, applied_force)

    @test isapprox(u, u_expected; atol=atol, rtol=rtol)
    @test isapprox(
        strain_energy_global,
        strain_energy_expected;
        atol=atol,
        rtol=rtol,
    )
end

8.5.1 Canonical regression case
The first case protects the established two-spring benchmark. It tests both the complete displacement vector u and strain_energy_global.
The displacement-vector test covers the assembled and constrained solution. The strain-energy test additionally covers the preservation and use of K_original before the constraint modification.


8.5.2 Noncanonical regression case
The second case calls:
solve_two_springs(2.0, 3.0, 12.0)
Before using its results as regression references, establish them independently from the analytical two-spring solution. With \(F=12\ \mathrm{N}\), \(k_1=2\ \mathrm{N/mm}\), and \(k_2=3\ \mathrm{N/mm}\),
\[
  u_3=\frac{F}{k_1}=6\ \mathrm{mm}
\]
and
\[
  u_1=\frac{F}{k_1}+\frac{F}{k_2}=10\ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
Therefore, in global-vector order,
\[
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  10\\
  0\\
  6
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm}.
\]
The corresponding total internal strain energy is
\[
  U=\frac{F^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2}\right)
   =60\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
\]
These independently established values are stored in the test file as the expected regression references. The case then checks that the callable analysis works for physical inputs other than the historical canonical benchmark.

title: 9  The weak form of the one-dimensional axial bar
text:
9.1 From three-dimensional equilibrium to a one-dimensional model
Part II introduced the finite element assembly process through discrete spring systems. For those systems, the element force–displacement relations followed directly from spring kinematics, the constitutive law, and equilibrium. Part III moves to continuum problems, where the unknown is a field governed by a differential equation. Before the familiar finite element assembly process can be used, the continuum problem must therefore be reformulated in a form suitable for numerical approximation.
The familiar algebraic system \(\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}\) will eventually reappear, but the path to it is now different: the governing differential equation is first reformulated in weak form and only then restricted to a finite-dimensional approximation. This formulation provides a systematic basis for handling spatially varying properties, distributed loads, natural boundary conditions, and finite element approximations of different orders. It therefore provides the bridge between the continuum model and the finite element equations that will ultimately be assembled.
In a general three-dimensional continuum, whether the deformation is small or finite and whether the material response is linear or nonlinear, the quasi-static equilibrium equation in the current configuration can be written as \[
  \nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0},
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) is the Cauchy stress tensor and \(\mathbf{b}\) is the body-force vector per unit current volume. The assumptions of small deformation and linear elasticity will be introduced later through the kinematic and constitutive relations. Throughout this book, the first stress index identifies the normal to the plane on which the stress acts, while the second identifies the direction of the stress component. With this convention, the Cartesian equilibrium equations are \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \frac{\partial \sigma_{xx}}{\partial x}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{yx}}{\partial y}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{zx}}{\partial z}
  +b_x &= 0,\\[4pt]
  \frac{\partial \sigma_{xy}}{\partial x}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{yy}}{\partial y}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{zy}}{\partial z}
  +b_y &= 0,\\[4pt]
  \frac{\partial \sigma_{xz}}{\partial x}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{yz}}{\partial y}
  +\frac{\partial \sigma_{zz}}{\partial z}
  +b_z &= 0.
  \end{aligned}
\] For the continuum model considered here, balance of angular momentum implies that the Cauchy stress tensor is symmetric (\(\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\mathsf T}\) or \(\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}\)). Together with kinematic relations, a constitutive law, and appropriate boundary conditions, the equilibrium equations define a boundary-value problem.
We now introduce a one-dimensional idealization of a slender three-dimensional body: the axial bar model. The bar is assumed to be slender, aligned with the \(x\) axis, and subjected to axial loading, as shown in Figure 9.1. Its deformation is described by an axial displacement field \(u(x)\), while the stress distribution over each cross-section is represented by the axial resultant \(N(x)\).
As discussed in Chapter 3, the one-dimensional bar model is based on a kinematic idealization: only the axial displacement is retained, and it is assumed to be uniform over each cross-section and to vary only along the bar axis. Lateral deformation, including effects such as Poisson contraction, is not represented by the one-dimensional model. The displacement field is therefore described by the scalar function
\[
  u=u(x).
\]
Under the small-strain assumption, the axial strain retained by the model is
\[
  \varepsilon(x)
  =
  \varepsilon_{xx}(x)
  =
  \frac{du}{dx}
  =
  u'(x).
\]
For a linearly elastic material,
\[
  \sigma(x)=E(x)\varepsilon(x).
\]
The internal axial force is obtained by integrating the axial stress over the cross-section,
\[
  N(x)=\int_{A(x)} \sigma\,dA.
\]
For the one-dimensional bar model, the axial stress is assumed to be uniform over each cross-section. The resultant therefore reduces to
\[
  N(x)=A(x)\sigma(x).
\]
Using the linear elastic constitutive relation \(\sigma(x)=E(x)\varepsilon(x)\) together with \(\varepsilon(x)=u'(x)\) gives
\[
  \boxed{
  N(x)=E(x)A(x)u'(x)
  }.
\]
Correspondingly, the distributed axial load \(q(x)\) represents the external load resultant per unit length of the bar. It may include contributions from body forces acting over the cross-section and from tractions applied to the lateral surface. We may therefore write
\[
  q(x)
  =
  \int_{A(x)} b_x\,dA
  +
  q_s(x),
\]
where \(q_s(x)\) denotes the axial load per unit length resulting from lateral surface tractions.
If the body-force density \(b_x(x)\) is uniform over the cross-section and no lateral traction is present, this reduces to
\[
  q(x)=A(x)b_x(x).
\]
Loads applied to the end cross-sections are treated separately as boundary forces.

9.2 Equilibrium and the strong form
Consider the equilibrium of an infinitesimal segment of the bar.






Figure 9.2: Equilibrium of an infinitesimal segment of the one-dimensional bar.



The quantity \(q(x)\,dx\) shown in Figure 9.2 represents the leading-order resultant of the distributed load over the infinitesimal segment. In the equilibrium equation below, we retain the exact resultant \(\int_x^{x+dx}q(s)\,ds\) before taking the limit \(dx\to0\).
We take \(N>0\) in tension and \(q>0\) when the distributed load acts in the positive \(x\) direction. With this sign convention, axial force equilibrium over the segment \([x,x+dx]\) gives
\[
  -N(x)+N(x+dx)+\int_x^{x+dx} q(s)\,ds=0.
\]
Dividing by \(dx\),
\[
  \frac{N(x+dx)-N(x)}{dx}
  +
  \frac{1}{dx}\int_x^{x+dx} q(s)\,ds
  =0.
\]
Taking the limit as \(dx\to0\) gives the local equilibrium equation
\[
  \boxed{
  \frac{dN}{dx}+q=0
  }.
\]
Using
\[
  N(x)=E(x)A(x)u'(x),
\]
we obtain the governing differential equation
\[
  \boxed{
  \frac{d}{dx}\left(EA\,u'\right)+q=0
  \qquad \text{in }\Omega=(0,L).
  }
\]
This form remains valid when \(E\), \(A\), or both vary along the bar. Only when \(EA\) is constant can it be reduced to
\[
  EA\,u''+q=0 \qquad \text{in }\Omega=(0,L).
\]






NoteElliptic character of the bar problem



The governing bar equation is the one-dimensional counterpart of the elliptic equations that arise in static elasticity.
In two and three dimensions, combining equilibrium, kinematics, and a stable elastic constitutive law leads to a coupled system of second-order elliptic partial differential equations for the displacement field. In the present one-dimensional setting, the corresponding problem reduces to a second-order ordinary differential equation.
For positive axial rigidity \(E(x)A(x)>0\) throughout the bar, the differential operator \[
  -\frac{d}{dx}
  \left(
  EA\,\frac{d}{dx}
  \right)
\]
is the one-dimensional analogue of an elliptic operator.


A differential equation alone does not define the problem completely. Boundary conditions are also required.
For the bar considered here, the left end is fixed,
\[
  u(0)=0,
\]
while the axial force prescribed at the right end is
\[
  N(L)=E(L)A(L)u'(L)=\bar F,
\]
with \(\bar F>0\) acting in the positive \(x\) direction.
The displacement condition is a Dirichlet, or essential, boundary condition. The force condition is a Neumann, or natural, boundary condition.
In general, the boundary \(\Gamma\) is partitioned into a displacement part \(\Gamma_u\) and a traction part \(\Gamma_t\). For the present one-dimensional problem,
\[
  \Gamma_u=\{0\},
  \qquad
  \Gamma_t=\{L\}.
\]
The prescribed displacement on \(\Gamma_u\) is \(u=0\), while the prescribed traction resultant on \(\Gamma_t\) is \(N=\bar F\).
The governing differential equation, together with the associated boundary conditions, constitutes the strong form of the boundary-value problem.

text:
9.3 Why introduce a weak form?
The strong form imposes the governing differential equation pointwise and therefore places relatively strong smoothness requirements on the displacement field.
As an example, consider a perfectly bonded bar made of two materials. If the axial rigidity \(EA\) changes abruptly across the material interface, equilibrium requires the axial force
\[
  N=EA\,u'
\]
to remain continuous in the absence of an interface load. Because perfect bonding also requires the displacement \(u\) to remain continuous, a nonzero transmitted axial force produces different displacement gradients on the two sides of the interface whenever the values of \(EA\) differ. Thus, \(u\) remains continuous while \(u'\) is generally discontinuous across the interface, as illustrated in Figure 9.3.






Figure 9.3: Bimaterial axial bar with \(q=0\), piecewise-constant axial rigidities, and \(E_2A_2>E_1A_1\). Perfect bonding keeps the displacement \(u\) continuous, while equilibrium requires the transmitted axial force \(N=EA\,u'\) to remain continuous. The region with greater axial rigidity therefore has the smaller displacement gradient, so \(u'\) jumps across the material interface.



The appropriate divergence form of the equilibrium equation is
\[
  \frac{d}{dx}\left(EA\,u'\right)+q=0,
\]
rather than the expanded form \(EA\,u''+q=0\), which is valid only where \(EA\) is constant.
In this example, the physical equilibrium condition remains perfectly valid: the axial force \(N=EA\,u'\) is continuous across the interface. What changes is the regularity of the displacement field. Because \(u'\) is discontinuous across the material interface, the displacement field \(u\) does not have a classical second derivative at the interface.
The difficulty is therefore related to the smoothness required to enforce the strong form pointwise. A weak formulation expresses the same equilibrium problem while requiring fewer derivatives of the displacement field. As we will see shortly, equilibrium is no longer enforced pointwise; instead, it is imposed in a weighted, integral sense over the domain. In the standard displacement-based finite element formulation used here, this allows the displacement approximation to remain continuous while its derivatives may be discontinuous across material interfaces or element boundaries. The first step toward this formulation is to replace pointwise enforcement of the differential equation by a weighted integral statement.

text:
9.4 The weighted residual statement
Define the residual of the governing equation as
\[
  r(u)
  =
  \frac{d}{dx}\left(EA\,u'\right)+q.
\]
The strong form requires
\[
  r(u)=0
  \qquad
  \text{at every point in }\Omega.
\]
Rather than requiring the strong form to hold pointwise, we introduce a test, or weight, function \(w(x)\) and require the weighted residual to vanish for every admissible test function: \[
  \boxed{
  \int_0^L w\,r(u)\,dx=0
  \qquad
  \forall\,w\in V.
  }
\]
Here, admissible means that the function has the regularity required by the formulation and satisfies the relevant essential boundary conditions; the precise test space will be defined below.






NoteTrial, test, and admissible functions



The trial field is a candidate for the unknown displacement field \(u\).
A test function, also called a weight function, is used to test the equilibrium statement through the weighted residual or weak form.
A function is admissible when it has the required regularity and satisfies the appropriate essential boundary conditions. For trial fields this means \(u=\bar u\) on \(\Gamma_u\), where \(\bar u\) denotes the prescribed displacement; for test functions it means the corresponding homogeneous condition \(w=0\) on \(\Gamma_u\).
The same test function \(w\) appearing in the weighted residual statement may also be interpreted as an admissible variation of the displacement field: a perturbation that does not violate the prescribed displacement.
More specifically, let \(u\) be an admissible displacement field satisfying
\[
  u=\bar u
  \qquad \text{on }\Gamma_u.
\]
A perturbed field can be written as
\[
  u+\eta w,
\]
where \(\eta\) is an arbitrary scalar. For the perturbed field to satisfy the same prescribed displacement, we must also have
\[
  u+\eta w=\bar u
  \qquad \text{on }\Gamma_u.
\]
Since \(u=\bar u\) on \(\Gamma_u\), this condition reduces to
\[
  \eta w=0
  \qquad \text{on }\Gamma_u.
\]
Because \(\eta\) is arbitrary, the test function must therefore satisfy
\[
  w=0
  \qquad \text{on }\Gamma_u.
\]
Thus, trial fields satisfy the prescribed essential boundary condition, whereas test functions satisfy the corresponding homogeneous condition.


Here \(V\) denotes the set of admissible test functions; it will be defined precisely below. For the axial bar,
\[
  \int_0^L
  w
  \left[
  \frac{d}{dx}\left(EA\,u'\right)+q
  \right]
  dx
  =0
  \qquad
  \forall\,w\in V.
\]
It is not enough for one weighted average of the residual to vanish. The integral relation must hold for every admissible test function. Before discretization, this is still an infinite family of conditions.
At this stage the derivative order acting on \(u\) has not changed. The next step is what makes the formulation useful for standard displacement-based finite elements.

text:
9.5 Integration by parts
Integration by parts transfers one derivative from the equilibrium term to the test function:
\[
  \int_0^L
  w\,\frac{d}{dx}\left(EA\,u'\right)dx
  =
  \left[wEAu'\right]_0^L
  -
  \int_0^L
  w'EAu'\,dx.
\]
The weighted residual statement therefore becomes
\[
  -\int_0^L
  w'EAu'\,dx
  +
  \int_0^L
  wq\,dx
  +
  \left[wEAu'\right]_0^L
  =0,
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
  \int_0^L
  w'EAu'\,dx
  =
  \int_0^L
  wq\,dx
  +
  \left[wEAu'\right]_0^L.
\]
This step has two consequences that are central to the finite element method:

the highest derivative acting on the displacement field has been reduced from second order to first order;
the boundary-force contribution has appeared explicitly.

No finite element approximation has yet been introduced: the weighted residual statement and the integration-by-parts step reformulate the continuum problem before any discretization is chosen.

9.6 Essential and natural boundary conditions
The trial displacement field must satisfy the prescribed displacement condition
\[
  u(0)=0.
\]
Test functions represent admissible variations of the trial field. They must therefore leave the prescribed displacement unchanged and satisfy the corresponding homogeneous condition. For the present problem,
\[
  w(0)=0.
\]
The boundary term generated by integration by parts then becomes
\[
  \left[wEAu'\right]_0^L
  =
  w(L)EAu'(L)-w(0)EAu'(0)
  =
  w(L)EAu'(L).
\]
Using the prescribed axial force
\[
  E(L)A(L)u'(L)=\bar F,
\]
we obtain
\[
  \boxed{
  \int_0^L
  w'EAu'\,dx
  =
  \int_0^L
  wq\,dx
  +
  w(L)\bar F
  \qquad
  \forall\,w\in V.
  }
\]
The distinction between the two boundary-condition types is now explicit. The essential condition constrains the admissible displacement field and therefore the admissible test functions. The natural condition enters the formulation through the boundary term generated by integration by parts.
This distinction also explains the terminology: essential conditions must be imposed on the admissible displacement space, whereas natural conditions arise naturally through the boundary term of the weak formulation.

text:
9.7 Regularity and admissible functions
The strong form requires the differential equation to hold pointwise. In a region where \(EA\) is differentiable and \(u\) is twice differentiable, the product rule gives
\[
  (EA)'u' + EA\,u'' + q = 0,
\]
which explicitly involves the second derivative of the displacement. More generally, a classical strong formulation requires \((EAu')'\) to exist pointwise. After integration by parts, the weak form contains only first derivatives of the trial and test functions.
For the present problem, the natural regularity space is the Sobolev space \(H^1(\Omega)\). Informally, a function belongs to \(H^1(\Omega)\) when both the function and its first weak derivative are square integrable. For the displacement field, with \(u'\) understood in the weak sense, this means
\[
  \int_\Omega
  \left(
  u^2+(u')^2
  \right)dx
  <\infty.
\]
A weak derivative generalizes the classical derivative by allowing differentiation to be defined in an integral sense rather than pointwise everywhere. This is important for finite elements: a continuous piecewise-linear displacement field belongs to \(H^1(\Omega)\) even though its derivative may jump at element boundaries.






NoteWhat is a weak derivative?



A classical derivative is defined pointwise. At a point where the slope is discontinuous, the classical derivative does not exist.
A weak derivative is defined instead through an integral relation. A function \(g\) is the weak derivative of \(u\) if
\[
  \int_\Omega u\,\varphi'\,dx
  =
  -\int_\Omega g\,\varphi\,dx
\]
for every smooth auxiliary function \(\varphi\) with compact support in \(\Omega\), meaning that \(\varphi\) vanishes in a neighborhood of the boundary.
The function \(\varphi\) used here is only an auxiliary function in the definition of the weak derivative; it should not be confused with the finite element test function \(w\) used in the weak formulation.
Consider a continuous piecewise-linear function with an interior point \(x_i\):
\[
  u(x)=
  \begin{cases}
  a_1x+b_1, & x<x_i,\\
  a_2x+b_2, & x>x_i
  \end{cases}
\]
with the coefficients chosen so that the two branches meet continuously at \(x_i\):
\[
  a_1x_i+b_1=a_2x_i+b_2.
\]
If \(a_1\neq a_2\), the classical derivative is not defined at \(x_i\). Away from that point,
\[
  g(x)=
  \begin{cases}
  a_1, & x<x_i,\\
  a_2, & x>x_i.
  \end{cases}
\]
This piecewise-constant function is nevertheless the weak derivative of \(u\). The value assigned to the derivative at the single point \(x_i\) does not affect the integrals appearing in the weak formulation.
This is why a continuous finite element displacement field may belong to \(H^1(\Omega)\) even though its derivative is discontinuous at element boundaries.


The standard displacement-based finite element approximations considered here are constructed to satisfy \(C^0\) continuity as the minimum interelement continuity requirement: the displacement field itself is continuous across element boundaries, whereas continuity of its derivatives is not imposed.
The superscript \(h\) will denote quantities associated with the finite-dimensional discretization. The symbol \(h\) is conventionally related to a characteristic element size; its precise meaning will become clear once the bar is partitioned into finite elements.
Thus,
\[
  u^h\in C^0(\Omega),
\]
while
\[
  \frac{du^h}{dx}
\]
may be discontinuous from one element to the next. As will be shown later, the weak form therefore admits the \(C^0\) piecewise-polynomial displacement fields used in standard finite elements, without requiring a classical second derivative to exist at element boundaries.
We can now define the admissible trial and test sets precisely. For the present problem, the prescribed displacement is homogeneous, so
\[
  S=
  \left\{
  u\in H^1(\Omega):
  u=0\text{ on }\Gamma_u
  \right\},
\]
while
\[
  V=
  \left\{
  w\in H^1(\Omega):
  w=0\text{ on }\Gamma_u
  \right\}.
\]
More generally, if a nonzero displacement \(u=\bar u\) is prescribed on \(\Gamma_u\), the trial set becomes
\[
  S=
  \left\{
  u\in H^1(\Omega):
  u=\bar u\text{ on }\Gamma_u
  \right\},
\]
while the test space \(V\) contains the corresponding homogeneous variations.

title: 9  The weak form of the one-dimensional axial bar
text:
9.8 The weak form
Define the bilinear form
\[
  a(w,u)
  =
  \int_0^L
  w'EAu'\,dx
\]
and the linear form
\[
  \ell(w)
  =
  \int_0^L
  wq\,dx
  +
  w(L)\bar F.
\]
The weak problem is therefore
\[
  \boxed{
  \text{Find }u\in S
  \text{ such that }
  a(w,u)=\ell(w)
  \qquad
  \forall\,w\in V.
  }
\]
The weak form expresses the same equilibrium problem as the strong form, but with lower regularity requirements. The natural boundary condition enters naturally through the load functional, or linear functional, \(\ell(w)\).

section: 9.9 From the weak problem to a finite-dimensional problem
text:
9.9 From the weak problem to a finite-dimensional problem
The weak problem is still infinite-dimensional because the admissible trial and test sets contain infinitely many functions.
The conforming finite element method used here replaces these sets by finite-dimensional approximations,
\[
  S^h\subset S,
  \qquad
  V^h\subset V.
\]
Informally, a finite-dimensional approximation is described by a finite number of coefficients. For the present bar problem, whose prescribed displacement is zero, the approximate displacement can be written as
\[
  u^h(x)
  =
  \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\,\phi_i(x),
\]
where the finite set of functions \(\phi_i(x)\) defines the approximation and the coefficients \(c_i\) are the unknowns.
For nonhomogeneous essential boundary conditions, the approximate field is written as the sum of a part satisfying the prescribed displacement and a homogeneous expansion for the remaining unknown part.
The choice of the functions \(\phi_i\) is part of the approximation. In the finite element method, they are typically constructed from piecewise polynomials defined over the elements. Other numerical methods may use different finite-dimensional spaces, for example spaces generated by trigonometric functions or global polynomials.
The finite-dimensional weak problem is obtained by seeking
\[
  u^h\in S^h
\]
such that
\[
  a(w^h,u^h)=\ell(w^h)
  \qquad
  \forall\,w^h\in V^h.
\]
This is a Galerkin approximation. In the standard displacement-based finite element method used here, the trial and test functions are constructed from the same finite-dimensional family of basis functions, after accounting for the essential boundary conditions. This choice is known as the Bubnov–Galerkin method.
Other formulations may use different approximation spaces for the trial and test functions; these are generally referred to as Petrov–Galerkin methods.
The remaining question is how those finite-dimensional spaces should be constructed so that the weak problem becomes a computable finite element model.

text:
Declarative programming
A programming paradigm in which the desired result is specified without explicitly prescribing the sequence of operations required to obtain it. In other words, declarative programming focuses on what should be achieved, while the underlying implementation determines how to achieve it. For example, selecting all even values from an array using a filtering operation expresses the desired result without explicitly defining the iteration and state changes required to construct it.
See also: Imperative programming. Further details: Wikipedia — Declarative programming.

title: Glossary
text:
I

Immutable object
An object whose contents or internal state cannot be changed after it has been created. An operation that appears to modify an immutable object instead creates a new object representing the modified value, leaving the original object unchanged. Strings and numbers are common examples of immutable objects in many programming languages.
See also: Mutable object; Modified in place.


Imperative programming
A programming paradigm in which a computation is expressed as an explicit sequence of commands that describe how a result should be obtained. Imperative programs typically modify variables or other aspects of the program state as execution proceeds. For example, selecting all even values from an array by iterating through its elements, testing each value, and adding the matching values to a new array follows an imperative approach.
See also: Declarative programming. Further details: Wikipedia — Imperative programming.

title: Glossary
text:
M

Modified in place
Describes an operation that changes an existing object or data structure directly, rather than creating and returning a separate modified copy.
For example, in Julia, integers are immutable:
x = 4
x = x + 1
Here, x is not modified in place. Instead, x is rebound from the value 4 to the new value 5.
By contrast, an array is mutable:
x = [4]
x[1] += 1
Here, the existing array is modified in place, changing its contents from [4] to [5].
See also: Mutable object; Immutable object.


Mutable object
An object whose contents or internal state can be changed after it has been created. Operations on a mutable object may therefore modify the existing object directly rather than creating a new one. Lists and dictionaries are common examples of mutable objects in many programming languages.
See also: Immutable object; Modified in place.

R

Refactoring
Restructuring existing code to improve its organization, readability, or reuse while preserving its intended computational behavior.

title: Glossary

S

Separation of concerns
A software-design principle in which different aspects of a program are kept in distinct parts of the code so that each part addresses a specific concern. For example, a numerical function can perform a finite element operation while diagnostic output is handled separately.
Further details: Wikipedia — Separation of concerns.
